newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Business chokes as rebels cut off Zaire capital.
newsitem.headline: Business chokes as rebels cut off Zaire capital.

text.p: Businesses are going bust in Zaire's sprawling capital, cut off by rebels from the most productive parts of the vast country and living in the shadow of impending siege, industrialists said on Sunday.

"The economy in Kinshasa is like a headless chicken. The body is still twitching, the head clucking but sooner or later it will stop," Joseph Kabeya, commercial adviser to ICCI group, one of Zaire's biggest rice and sugar importers, told Reuters.
"Businesses whose networks stretched across the country, are being choked, and with them the banks," a senior Zairean banker said.
On the vast Zaire river, the country's main conduit for internal and external trade, barges bob up and down at rusty ports, unused.
Shippers and traders no longer dare set sail to fetch and sell produce on the river and its many tributaries, which have long compensated for the collapse of Zaire's road network.

Instead the river has become a line of advance for rebels fighting to end President Mobutu Sese Seko's 32-year rule, and a path of retreat for demoralised government forces looting their way back from the battlefield.

"The economic tissue was already diseased. Now some businesses have lost 80 percent of their existing markets. We are being progressively asphyxiated," said Jose Endundo, president of the Zairean business association, ANEZA.

Since Laurent Kabila's rebels launched the war seven months ago in the east of the country, Kinshasa has been progressively severred from Zaire's most productive agricultural and mineral regions as rebels took town after town.
Now only three of Zaire's 11 provinces remain in reach of Kinshasa, and those three are threatened by guerrillas who say they will soon march in force on the capital itself.

"A military operation on Kinshasa would have incalculable consequences. There's a risk that no one would come out the winner," cautioned Endundo, who is also the chief executive of the country's leading private airline, Zaire Airlines.
Meanwhile businesses, some down to 10 percent of normal activity according to Endundo, are being forced to lay off many employees.
Businessmen fear rebels intend to slowly suffocate the city in order to force Mobutu to step down, an uncomprimising demand of Kabila.
With access to the vast interior blocked, Kinshasa relies to a great extent on its imports which travel by train and road across a strip of land stretching west to the Atlantic ocean.
Should this line of supply be cut, traders say that food, petrol and even electricity shortages could swiftly be felt, with all the subsequent risks of a social explosion.
Existing stocks of most vital commodities in the capital are already low after retail traders allowed them to dwindle for fear of looting by unpaid soldiers.

Signs that the purchasing power of the impoverished inhabitants is disappearing as the capital is drained of liquid cash, the bulk of which used to come from the diamond and copper mining areas, are already there.
Zaireans, who despite years of political and economic crisis have rarely lost the ability to forget their sorrows, are deserting at night the city's once thriving bars and clubs.
For Endundo, the tragic consequences of years of economic mismanagement and state corruption which left even Mobutu's army virtually unpaid, are now being felt with full force.
"People have spoken a lot about politics. But you cannot eat politics. This country has committed serious errors in the economic sector and we are paying for this in a tragic way."
One positive aspect he draws from the current crisis is that the war has provoked an upsurge in nationalist sentiment.
Seven months ago, pundits were forecasting that the vast provinces of the interior neglected for so long by the central administration in the capital would secede.
Now, should the war come to an end and the fracture between rebel-held and government-held areas be mended, he predicts the country might stand a real chance of reconstructing as a whole.
